q: We made the perfect routines that allowed for rest and connection, and I absolutely love being in midwifery care. Seeing my people every week to care for me, my body, and baby just feels so sacred.
cx: A homebirth midwife, days after her third birth, misses being pregnant with two toddlers at home.

q: This new person who lives on 3-5 hours of sleep with sore boobs and no more weekly prenatal visits, doesn’t yet feel like me.
cx: Four days postpartum, the loss of the pregnancy routine.

q: I actually have a resource list on my website of everything from cpr classes to pelvic floor, therapists, sleep consultants, lactation consultants, feeding ots. But I will make up a list of baby must haves as well.
cx: A newly independent postpartum doula plans welcome baskets for clients.

q: FWIW, I paid for them to take a grandparents' class before my toddler was born, so none of the basic care requirements (feeding, diapering, car seat safety) should be news to them.
cx: Pregnant with her second; her parents still ignore her instructions when minding the toddler.

q: And I'm so sick of hearing how I "turned out just fine."
cx: Her parents' answer to her care rules.

q: I gave birth to my second late February so it’s been a huge help to have her around to do stuff with my kiddo while I stay home/take care of the baby. In the early days she was at my house/taking my toddler to the library/park/on errands 4-5 days a week.
cx: Her newly retired mother minds the toddler after the second birth.

q: I am super grateful for her help as it has made post partum very smooth for me. While I know there’s a certain amount of leeway when it comes to letting her be a grandma, I’m feeling very disrespected. It’s amazing not having to pay for day care but at this point I’m honestly really upset that these very boundaries are constantly being pushed.
cx: Free grandparent childcare that ignores her rules on screens and food.

q: people have asked me; “Where is the baby?” (I’m like … obviously with his father? Where else would he be…?) Meanwhile, when my partner takes the baby to the shop or etc, people say to him: “Ahhh, are you giving mum a break?”
cx: UK, six weeks in; the couple share care equally and strangers react.

q: My partner is self-employed and has fewer hours of work than most people but at a relatively generous rate. This means he’s been doing as few as 15 hours work a week and is home with me the rest of the time - we are lucky to have this flexibility
cx: Why equal care has been possible for them.

q: It’s actually a really good book and not crunchy, but the author goes through extreme anxiety and self-martyrdom - feeling bad about leaving the child for even a quick swim.
cx: On Lucy Jones's book Matrescence, which made her wonder if her lack of guilt was unusual.

q: I mentioned to my wife about possibly putting our son in daycare, but the price makes it questionably affordable without finding an opening in the local church/daycare/private school that is more affordable.
cx: Father on night shifts; in-laws mind their 13-month-old for free as a second baby comes.

q: We appreciate the help, and with free help I do feel there is some tradeoff that not EVERYTHING will be done the way you do it or want it done. But I feel like some lines are being crossed.
cx: Weighing free grandparent care against their own rules.

q: My mom said she wanted to help plan it, help with the registry, and book the room at a church. But weeks went by and nothing got done. Eventually she basically told me if “I” wanted the room, it would cost $200, so I paid for it myself.
cx: First baby due late August; family members drop out of a shower planned for four months.

q: Then I asked when the concert was and she told me it’s on my due date. When I got upset, she acted like I was being unreasonable because “babies usually don’t come on the exact due date anyway.”
cx: Her mother booked concert tickets for the due date.

q: This has been the first time I've ever encountered a midwife of any sort and I had no idea what that credential meant until posting her.
cx: US, 30 weeks, rotating through a practice's providers; unsure what a nurse-midwife is trained to do.
